item.research_question: How do additive manufacturing processing parameters and feedstock material types (pre-alloyed vs. mixed elemental) influence the microstructure, phase composition, density, and mechanical properties of high entropy alloys?
item.material_system: CrMnFeCoNi, AlCrFeCoNi, Al0.3CrFeCoNi, FeCoCrNi, NbMoTaW, VNbMoTaW, AlXCrFeCoNi, AlXCrFeNi2Cu, TiZrHfNb, FeCoNiCr, and composites with TiC or W reinforcement
item.processing_route: Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF, EB-PBF), Direct Energy Deposition (BPD, WAAM, WLAM), Binder Jetting, and Material Extrusion; parameters include laser energy density, scan velocity, layer thickness, hatch spacing, pre-heating (up to 1100 °C), and post-processing sintering or annealing (e.g., 900 °C, 1100 °C)
item.test_conditions: As-built conditions and post-heat treatment conditions; high-temperature oxidation testing; corrosion testing in harsh environments; tensile testing for yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
key_findings: L-PBF produces the highest yield strength and UTS in CrMnFeCoNi due to high cooling rates, but results in reduced elongation compared to DED.
Annealing at 900 °C decomposes dislocation networks in FeCoCrNi, reducing residual stress, while 1100 °C further reduces stress and forms twin-rich grains.
Using mixed elemental powder in PBF requires higher laser energy density than pre-alloyed powder to achieve adequate synthesis and density.
EB-PBF pre-heating (up to 1100 °C) causes element segregation in AlCrFeCoNi, leading to a higher fraction of FCC phase at the bottom of the part compared to the top.
Adding Al (X=0.75) to AlXCrFeNi2Cu HEA via L-PBF forms a cellular FCC dendrite with a B2 matrix, reducing crack propagation compared to the columnar FCC structure of the base alloy.
CrFeCoNi pre-alloyed powder mixed with Cu and Ti powders showed optimal energy density varying due to melting point differences (CrFeCoNi: 1414 °C, Cu: 1084 °C, Ti: 1688 °C).
Sintering AlCrFeCoNi at 900 °C in Binder Jetting forms an undesired sigma phase, while sintering above 1200 °C results in a single BCC phase.
Higher energy density in L-PBF reduces defects like pores, enhancing corrosion resistance in AlCrFeCoNi, whereas EB-PBF pre-heating can create Cr-depleted pitting sites.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that rapid solidification in L-PBF prevents element segregation but creates high residual stress and dislocation networks, while the thermal cycles in DED and pre-heating in EB-PBF act as in-situ heat treatments causing segregation and phase transformations (e.g., BCC to FCC). The synthesis of HEAs from mixed elemental powders is hindered by different melting points and segregation tendencies, requiring higher energy density for in-situ alloying. Post-processing heat treatments modify microstructures by relieving stress, recrystallizing grains, or inducing secondary phase formation depending on temperature and atmosphere.
item.limitations: The text states that synthesizing HEAs using mixed elemental powder remains challenging due to elemental segregation and different melting points. Imperfections such as volume defects and elemental segregation can serve as corrosion initiation sites. EB-PBF pre-heating causes microstructural changes between the bottom and top sections. The fabrication of pre-alloyed wires is significantly more expensive and complex. Inadequate parameters can lead to over-melting, vaporization, or incomplete fusion.
item.future_work: The authors emphasize the need for further research on lightweight HEAs and regular updates on the latest developments. They propose that future success should focus on adequate synthesis and physical properties, specifically regarding microstructural defects, and recommend using mixed elemental substances or combined cable wires to reduce costs while ensuring proper selection of grain size, morphology, and wire diameters.
quotes: synthesizing HEAs such as CrFeCoNi and CrMnFeCoNi HEAs by AM using mixed elemental powder remains challenging due to issues such as elemental segregation and the different melting points of the elements
The L-PBF process demonstrated an increase in strength compared to both L-DED and AMF processes.
The major limitation of all the main AM processes concerns the critical effect of the printing parameters on the properties of the final product.
